title: How the Axis of Resistance Recovered
gist: Five months into the U.S.-Iran war, the 'octopus doctrine' — kill the head in Tehran and the proxies die — has failed because the axis of resistance is now a self-reproducing web with distributed manufacturing, training, and procurement rather than a hub-and-spoke system. Axis groups build $1,500 Ababil-T drones from Chinese commercial parts bought on Alibaba, the Houthis have imposed a de facto blockade on Saudi Red Sea ports and struck Saudi energy infrastructure, and the authors argue the decisive chokepoints for drone proliferation sit in China, outside U.S. control.

insights.claim: The U.S.-Israeli campaign launched in late February 2026 rested on a theory that destroying Iran's leadership, economy, and supply lines would collapse the regime and its allies together, and five months of strikes have disproved it.
insights.speaker: Peter Salisbury
insights.so_what: Positions built on a fast Iranian capitulation — including short-dated energy risk premia — are mispriced against a network that regenerates.
insights.quote: Sever the head of the octopus in Tehran, the theory went, and the axis groups—the octopus’s many arms—would shrivel and die, too.

insights.claim: The axis has shifted from a hub-and-spoke system routed through Tehran to a densely interconnected, self-reproducing web where knowledge, resources, and decision-making are pooled in multiple places simultaneously, eliminating identifiable points of failure.
insights.speaker: Peter Salisbury
insights.so_what: Decapitation and interdiction strategies have no target set that produces cascading collapse; assume attrition, not breakage.
insights.quote: Today, it more closely resembles a densely interconnected, self-reproducing web, in which knowledge, resources, and even decision-making can be pooled in many different places at the same time.

insights.claim: The axis survived a sequence of shocks that should have been fatal under the old model — Hamas's decimation in Gaza, Nasrallah's killing and Hezbollah command losses in September 2024, the Assad regime's collapse in Syria, and the 12-day war of June 2025 — and remained largely intact.
insights.speaker: Peter Salisbury
insights.so_what: Four sequential decapitation events with no network collapse is strong evidence the resilience is structural rather than luck.
insights.locator: Even after Israel’s devastation of Hamas

insights.claim: Outright defeat of Iran and the axis groups is likely out of reach, so the achievable objective is limiting the threat rather than eliminating it.
insights.speaker: Peter Salisbury
insights.so_what: The base case is an indefinite, containable-but-persistent conflict — not resolution — which argues for a structurally elevated Middle East risk premium.
insights.quote: Washington can no longer fall back on political pressure, sanctions, and military strikes.

themes.theme: Deliberate upskilling: from insurgents to military-industrial bases

insights.claim: The IRGC runs a graduated capability ladder in which would-be axis members receive basic training, battlefield-proven groups get advanced weapons including one-way attack drones, and a small trusted subset is taught to build its own weapons from self-imported parts.
insights.speaker: Peter Salisbury
insights.so_what: A tiered franchise model means capability spreads predictably; the tier a group occupies forecasts its future reach.
insights.locator: UPSKILLING THE AXIS

insights.claim: Hamas, Hezbollah, and the Houthis can each now build and field their own one-way attack drones with a reach of up to 1,600 miles, putting most Gulf and eastern Mediterranean infrastructure inside range of non-state actors.
insights.speaker: Peter Salisbury
insights.so_what: A 1,600-mile non-state strike radius means Gulf energy, desalination, and shipping assets carry a permanent standoff-attack risk independent of Iranian state decisions.
insights.quote: Today, Hamas, Hezbollah, and the Houthis can all build and field their own one-way attack drones, firing them at targets up to 1,600 miles away.

insights.claim: Axis groups have assembled their own rosters of smugglers, businesspeople, traders, and engineers and now perform the functions of the military-industrial bases of rich, powerful states despite appearing loosely intertwined to outsiders.
insights.speaker: Peter Salisbury
insights.so_what: These are procurement and manufacturing organizations, not militias — the right analytical comparison is a defense industrial base, not an insurgency.

insights.claim: Training has been subcontracted outward: in 2010 all documented Hezbollah drone training happened in Iran under Iranian instructors, by 2015 Hezbollah was training Hamas, the Houthis, and Iraqi militias, and by 2026 the Houthis were teaching al-Shabab basic drone flying at sites in Yemen.
insights.speaker: Peter Salisbury
insights.so_what: Knowledge transfer is now peer-to-peer and expanding into the Horn of Africa and Sudan — the proliferation frontier has moved beyond the Middle East.
insights.quote: In 2010, for example, all documented drone training for Hezbollah took place in Iran and was led by Iranian instructors.

insights.claim: Since at least 2025 Tehran has supplied Islamic Resistance in Iraq groups with a steady flow of Shahed-101 and Shahed-107 drones used against U.S. bases and Gulf state infrastructure over the past six months.
insights.speaker: Peter Salisbury
insights.so_what: Named munition types and a supply cadence give a concrete signature to watch for in future attribution of Gulf infrastructure strikes.

insights.claim: Sanctions and terrorism designations worked when the United States and its allies controlled most exports, trade routes, and financial networks needed to move arms, and that structural precondition no longer holds.
insights.speaker: Peter Salisbury
insights.so_what: Sanctions efficacy is a function of chokepoint ownership; as manufacturing shifts to China, expect declining returns from every new designation round.
insights.locator: At the turn of this century, these tools were useful

insights.claim: The Houthis had already begun building their own weapons by 2024, contradicting American and European officials who told the authors the group's arsenal came mainly from Iranian dhow smuggling.
insights.speaker: Peter Salisbury
insights.so_what: Official Western assessments of proxy supply lines lagged reality by years, so current interdiction-based confidence should be discounted.

insights.speaker: Peter Salisbury
insights.so_what: Hezbollah's replacement pipeline was already European-routed before the Syrian land bridge closed, which is why cutting Syria did not degrade it.

insights.claim: New supply lines ship parts separately across the globe and assemble them near the point of use, which structurally neutralizes designation-based enforcement aimed at named entities and shipments.
insights.speaker: Peter Salisbury
insights.so_what: Component-level dispersion is the specific mechanism defeating sanctions — countermeasures must target dual-use components, not organizations.

insights.claim: Between five million and six million shipping containers move on the high seas daily, and parts are bought by anonymous shell companies in secrecy jurisdictions and routed through trade hubs that prioritize ease of doing business over cargo screening.
insights.speaker: Peter Salisbury
insights.so_what: The screening problem is a needle-in-haystack at a scale no enforcement budget can cover, which is why the authors pivot to supplier-side controls.
insights.quote: five million to six million shipping containers that navigate the high seas daily

insights.claim: When shell companies are sanctioned, their owners simply shut them down and register new ones, making designation a cost of doing business rather than a barrier.
insights.speaker: Peter Salisbury
insights.so_what: Designation counts are a activity metric, not an effectiveness metric — do not read rising sanctions volume as tightening pressure.

insights.claim: Chinese manufacturers now produce the intermediate goods needed to build drones at increasing scale and shrinking cost, and Beijing does not restrict sale of many weaponizable parts on the grounds they are civilian goods.
insights.speaker: Peter Salisbury
insights.so_what: The bottleneck for global drone proliferation now sits inside Chinese commercial supply chains, giving Beijing a lever it currently has no incentive to pull.
insights.locator: But Chinese manufacturers now produce

insights.claim: Iran and axis groups can assemble the Ababil-T, historically the axis workhorse drone, from readily available Chinese-origin parts sourced on commercial sites such as Alibaba for about $1,500 per unit.
insights.speaker: Peter Salisbury
insights.so_what: A $1,500 unit cost against multimillion-dollar interceptors is an unsustainable defensive cost ratio — the economics favor the attacker indefinitely.
insights.quote: Iran and axis groups can build the Ababil-T, historically the workhorse drone of the axis fleet, from readily available Chinese-origin parts for about $1,500.

insights.claim: The barrier to fielding first-person-view drones against the Israel Defense Forces is now a credit card, YouTube instructional videos, and modest manufacturing skill.
insights.speaker: Peter Salisbury
insights.so_what: Capability no longer tracks state sponsorship, so interdicting Iranian transfers cannot by itself reduce the threat.
insights.quote: All Hezbollah needs to obtain and retrofit the first-person drones it has been using to target the Israel Defense Forces since early 2026 is a credit card, access to YouTube instructional videos, and a bit of manufacturing acumen.

insights.claim: Chinese and Iranian copies of drone engines once smuggled disguised as Jet Ski engines now power both the Russian and Iranian drone campaigns in Ukraine and the Middle East, linking the two theaters through one component supply chain.
insights.speaker: Peter Salisbury
insights.so_what: Ukraine and Middle East drone escalation share an upstream input, so pressure or disruption in one theater propagates to the other.

insights.claim: China has little near-term reason to help Washington curb drone-part sales, but is worried about drones as a domestic security threat, and entrepôts like the UAE that long looked the other way may be reconsidering after absorbing waves of Shahed-136s.
insights.speaker: Peter Salisbury
insights.so_what: The plausible path to component controls runs through Chinese domestic security anxiety and Gulf transshipment hubs, not through U.S. pressure.

insights.speaker: Peter Salisbury
insights.so_what: AIS-gap analytics around the Gulf of Oman are a concrete, trackable signal for Iranian materiel movement and sanctions evasion.

insights.claim: The shadow fleet network is connected through shell companies to a single repeatedly sanctioned Syrian businessman who has moved oil and money for Iran and Hezbollah, and its ships continue delivering to Houthi-controlled Yemeni ports.
insights.speaker: Peter Salisbury
insights.so_what: Repeated designation of the same node without disrupting the flow is direct evidence that entity-level sanctions are not binding.

insights.speaker: Peter Salisbury
insights.so_what: Libya has become a new Mediterranean transshipment node, opening a northern resupply route that Israeli interdiction is not currently postured to cover.

insights.speaker: Peter Salisbury
insights.so_what: Red Sea routing risk and Saudi energy asset risk are both live again; the 2025 truce that markets treated as durable proved reversible within a year.

themes.theme: What the authors argue Washington should do instead

insights.claim: The recommended strategy combines continued disruption of axis commercial and financial networks, splitting off peripheral groups not yet embedded in the ecosystem such as Horn of Africa recruits, and political engagement with established groups as they take on governance.
insights.speaker: Peter Salisbury
insights.so_what: Implies a policy path toward de facto recognition of axis groups as governing authorities, a material shift in the regional diplomatic baseline.
insights.locator: DEAL WITH IT

insights.claim: Adopting the IRGC's own playbook by building a U.S. array of state and nonstate proxies is dismissed as arduous and dangerous given Washington's spotty record building allied conventional forces and its tendency to discard allies once they stop being useful.
insights.speaker: Peter Salisbury
insights.so_what: Rules out the mirror-image response that hawkish policy circles will likely propose, narrowing realistic options to negotiation plus supply-side controls.
insights.locator: Alternatively, Washington could throw caution to the wind

insights.claim: The proposed structural fix is a multilateral initiative to track dual-use drone components with agreed penalties for transfers to nonstate armed groups, because the decisive chokepoints are not American-controlled.
insights.speaker: Peter Salisbury
insights.so_what: Any credible drone-proliferation regime requires Chinese participation, which makes it hostage to the broader U.S.-China relationship.
insights.quote: The chokepoints that matter for drone proliferation are not under U.S. control.
insights.locator: However it decides to deal with the axis

insights.claim: Deals with axis actors should take the form of structured agreements brokering country-level political settlements accompanied by U.S.-Iranian diplomacy, rather than narrow bilateral truces like the U.S.-Houthi agreement that broke down.
insights.speaker: Peter Salisbury
insights.so_what: The failure mode of the 2025 Houthi truce — a narrow bilateral deal reversed within a year — is the explicit template of what not to repeat.
insights.locator: Deals would not necessarily resemble bilateral agreements
